newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU strides towards new exchange rate mechanism.
newsitem.headline: EU strides towards new exchange rate mechanism.

text.p: The nuts and bolts of a new exchange rate mechanism that links a single European currency with those not participating in a monetary union are gradually falling into place.

European Union monetary sources say a meeting of the EU's monetary committee held last week made progress toward an accord where a future European Central Bank would play an active role in initiating parity changes of currencies outside economic and monetary union.

Work on a revamped European Rate Mechanism is primarily in the hands of the Frankfurt-based European Monetary Institute, forerunner to the Eurpean Central Bank, and officials say the Institute has gone far in defining the outline of such a system.
"The sense I get is that the EMI has made a lot of headway on defining the parameters of a new (currency) grid," said one EU monetary official.
Alexandre Lamfalussy, president of the EMI, will unveil the latest thinking on a European Rate Mechansim when he meets EU finance ministers and central bank governors in Dublin on Sept. 20 and 21.
To facilitate currency stability between the so-called ins and pre-ins, the ECB is seen acting as a watchdog for whenever a change in parity rates is needed among outside currencies.

The decision to give the ECB such a prominent role is a clear attempt to avoid the mistakes of the past when currency realignments were often made too late to adjust to changes in a country's economic fundamentals.
The present ERM underwent a crisis in 1992 which forced Britain and Italy out of the currency grid and led to costly intervention by central banks throughout the EU.

At present most currencies in the ERM can fluctuate within 15 percent of agreed central rates against other members of the mechanism. The exceptions are the mark and guilder, which move in a narrow 2.25 percent band.
Another key aspect of a new ERM is the acknowledgment that limits should be placed on ECB intervention to support a currency under speculative attack.
While officially there will be an understanding that intervention should be limitless, a so-called "escape clause" is under review which would constrain the Bank's responsibilities.

Monetary officials say there is a strong desire not to specify such limits in an attempt to keep financial markets guessing. Divulging the details might embolden markets when a currency came under downward pressure.
"I don't think you will see any specifics on this," said one official of the planned limits.

Nor will there be any news on the precise width of trading bands in which non-participating currencies will trade. Such decisions are considered premature and presumably will be made once the countries which take part in EMU are known.
A further item under consideration, related to parity changes, is to have EU finance ministers both inside and outside EMU to play role in initiating such decisions.
